text: The horse was undersized, which on a racetrack is an accounting problem before it is a sentiment. Gary Ross spends 141 minutes on the arithmetic around it: the men who buy, train and ride an animal in years when almost no one in America has money to lose, and a country reading its own odds in the results. One of the film's Academy Awards went to the editing, which is the right place to look — a race lasts two minutes, and everything a picture can say about one is settled by where the cuts fall, how long a stretch of dirt is allowed to run, when the crowd is let back in. Between races the film slows almost to portraiture, the Depression carried in worn cloth and low light rather than in figures. The uplift is on the label. The patience underneath it is the reason to sit down.

It is filed as a comedy, and the filing is not an error. Todd Solondz gives 140 minutes to a set of lives that keep passing within arm's reach of each other without touching, and lets each of them talk at length, in ordinary rooms, under an even light that offers no comment. The flatness is the method. Nothing in the staging tells a viewer how to feel about what is being confessed, so the laughs arrive a beat before the recognition of what was funny, and then sit there. Solondz's people are fluent about their own loneliness and heard by nobody; the cruelty and the sympathy come out of the same decision, which is to let them finish their sentences. The National Board of Review placed it among the ten best films of 1998, a fair measure of how quickly the shock was understood as craft.

A disused rail line in rural New Jersey, and a man who has moved out there precisely because nobody walks it. Solitude is his plan, thought through in advance and entirely defensible, and the film's business is watching it fail by inches. Tom McCarthy needs eighty-eight minutes and spends most of them on interruptions: a hot dog vendor who talks whether or not anyone answers, a woman carrying a loss she does not explain, both turning up at the wrong moment with unreasonable persistence. Being stared at in a small town is a daily condition here rather than an occasion for speeches. Sundance gave the film a special jury prize for acting, the honest award for a picture built out of three people adjusting their faces while somebody else speaks. Walking the tracks is a form of conversation. So is declining to.

Two people hold a claim on the same small California bungalow, and neither has broken a law. Behrani bought it at county auction as an asset to be repaired and resold, his son's tuition priced into the plaster. Kathy lost it to a clerical injustice and has nowhere else to be. Vadim Perelman keeps both of those true for two hours, which is the whole difficulty: sympathy cannot be spent on one without being taken from the other. Around the dispute the film assembles the machinery ordinary people reach for when they are in the right — a lawyer, a friendly police officer, a folder of documents — and shows how little of it was designed for a case where both sides are. The county's error is small, procedural and already filed away. Everything downstream of it belongs to the two households.

Two men arrive in the same town with identical black cases; one holds a guitar, the other holds guns. Everything in the following eighty-one minutes comes of nobody checking. Robert Rodriguez made it in Spanish, with a hero whose ambition goes no further than finding a bar that will pay him to sing, and built it as a chase on foot: a stranger, a drug lord's men, and streets narrow enough that survival means staying one corner ahead. The western bones are left showing, which is half the appeal — the genre stripped to the two or three parts it actually needs to run. It sits in the National Film Registry now, an odd destination for something assembled this fast. No fat, no explanations, and a guitar case carried through the entire thing like a debt.

A drift of snow stops the train, and with it any possibility that someone got off. What follows is one of the strictest shapes in popular fiction: a fixed number of passengers, a single carriage, and a detective who works by sitting down opposite each of them in turn. Sidney Lumet treats those interviews as the action — 1935 manners, two chairs, a courteous question, and the small adjustments a face makes while answering it. The period is carried on the surface, in tailoring and lacquer and the ritual of boarding, and the Academy's award for costume design was not a courtesy to the wardrobe department. Hercule Poirot wants symmetry and is given a corridor of accounts that do not agree. Outside, nothing moves for two hours. That stillness is the pressure.

A promise made to a grieving mother carries no legal weight, which is exactly why it holds. The man who makes this one is a police chief with days left on the job, an authority about to expire, and he keeps working after it does — off the books, unhurried, with nothing left to organise his time but the case. Sean Penn films it as a procedural cut loose from the department: no partner, no warrant, no shift ending, only a private conviction that the file is wrong. Two hours of that is a long test of patience, and the film knows it, letting errands and weeks pile up while the question stays where it was. The National Board of Review named it among the ten best of its year. What remains is the ordinary shape of a retirement quietly spent on somebody else's daughter.

Humbert Humbert is disgusted by American vulgarity and cannot stop looking at it, and the film treats those as one appetite rather than two. Adrian Lyne stages the arrival first: a boarding house, a landlady named Charlotte Haze, a British novelist with manners and condescension to spare, a household he means only to observe and begins managing within days. The difficulty of the material is that its narrator is charming and does his own narrating, so any adaptation must decide how much of that persuasion to lend the camera. Lyne keeps the surfaces warm and slow while the calculation stays audible in what Humbert tells himself. A hundred and thirty-seven minutes inside a man's justification is not a comfortable arrangement, and the discomfort is the work. It was made as a French production, in English, about a country watched from outside.

Two schoolgirls invent a kingdom out of novels and drawings and then start living in it more than outside it. Peter Jackson films the household around them plainly — meals, parents in doorways, a family newly settled in New Zealand — and then lets the invented country break through at full scale, as solid as the kitchen, holding the screen for minutes together. That is the argument of the picture: a friendship this absorbing does not escape the ordinary world, it competes with it and begins to win. Juliet supplies the talk, Pauline the writing. The adults can tell only that the pace of the house has changed and that the two of them have stopped explaining themselves. It runs 109 minutes and accelerates throughout, which is not the usual tempo for a film about two girls and their notebooks.

Seven years since the book that made his name, and Grady is still employed to teach other people how to write one. Curtis Hanson keeps returning to the joke inside that arrangement: a campus is the one workplace where failing at the job and performing it look identical, so a professor who cannot finish a sentence stands in front of students who cannot start one, and the term proceeds on schedule. Then a weekend hands him one misadventure after another, in the company of a young author with more nerve than manners. The adapted screenplay took an Academy Award, and its shape is the reason: farce played at low volume, each disaster arriving politely, alone, waiting to be let in. Comedies about writers usually flatter them. This one lets Grady be tiresome for a hundred and seven minutes and stays fond of him.

In 1962 the Academy still gave a separate award for black-and-white photography, and this film took it: flat grey light, a staircase, two faces held past comfort. Robert Aldrich confines almost all of 135 minutes to one decaying house in Hollywood, where a woman who was famous as a child performer looks after a sister who cannot walk, and the looking after has curdled. The horror is domestic and unhurried — rooms, stairs, trays, the arithmetic of who in the house is able to leave it. What an old fame has become is worn openly here, in what one sister puts on her face each morning, and Aldrich lets that stand without commentary or pity. Two women in one building, and neither is finished with the other.

Thirteen weeks is not long to change a person, and the film treats that as a deadline rather than a premise. Zack Mayo arrives at officer candidate school able to do everything except need anyone, and Sergeant Emil Foley, who recognises the type, applies pressure exactly there: not to the drills, which Mayo passes, but to the habit of holding every person at arm's length. Taylor Hackford runs the training and the romance on a single clock. A courtship conducted between inspections is also a question about week fourteen, and the affair founders on the same point the training does — he will not give anything away. The film is unembarrassed about its score, which took an Academy Award, and no more embarrassed about the effect it wants from it. Discipline here is not a metaphor. It is a schedule with an end date.

Summer of 1957: the company that carries his name is ten years old and close to insolvent. Michael Mann builds the film on that ledger rather than on speed. Enzo Ferrari must win races in order to sell cars, and must sell cars in order to build the ones that can win, and the loop is drawing tight. Laura built the firm with him from nothing, which means every argument at home is also an argument about the business. Between them sit one son who is dead and another who has not been acknowledged in public. Mann keeps the racing where an accountant would keep it, as expenditure and exposure, and keeps the mourning where it actually lives, in the running of a household. A hundred and thirty-one minutes of one man negotiating at once with a bank, a marriage, and the drivers he sends out in machines he made.

The obstacle in this romance is not feeling. It is staff. Andrew Shepherd is a widower who also runs the country, and every move available to an ordinary suitor — a phone call, a dinner, an evening nobody writes down — must pass through people employed to prevent precisely that. Rob Reiner plays the mismatch as comedy first, since Sydney Ellen Wade lobbies the administration for a living and the two of them already hold formal positions with respect to each other. Then the polling arrives, and a private matter turns into a figure that paid men worry over. What keeps the film honest is that it never argues the numbers are unfair; they are the arrangement he accepted. Its score won an Academy Award in the comedy category, fitting for a picture about two adults trying to be alone in a building designed against it.
